question: On four named binary tabular datasets (OpenML adult v2 [data_id 1590], bank-marketing [1461], electricity [151] and phoneme [1489], each capped at a stratified sample of at most 20,000 rows, with a calibration-split fraction fixed at the design gate so that every calibration split has at least 1,000 cases), how well calibrated are the predicted probabilities of logistic regression, random forests and gradient-boosted trees with library defaults (scikit-learn 1.9.1, no tuning), and how do Platt scaling and isotonic regression fitted on a held-out calibration split change log-loss, Brier score and calibration error, with the base model held fixed?
hypotheses: H1 (replication; Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana 2005): without recalibration, random forests have higher expected calibration error than logistic regression (15 equal-mass bins on P(y=1); tie handling at bin edges fixed at the design gate). Brier and log-loss are reported descriptively; Fonseca and Lopes (2017) report that on Brier score uncalibrated random forests often beat logistic regression. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.

H2a (contested in prior work): isotonic regression fitted on the held-out split lowers the Brier score of random forests relative to no recalibration. Log-loss (with a clipping epsilon fixed at the design gate, clip counts reported) and ECE are reported descriptively. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.

H2b (an extension of Fonseca and Lopes 2017): isotonic regression lowers the Brier score of scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier relative to no recalibration. Log-loss and ECE are reported descriptively. Decision rule per dataset (fixed now): for each of 10 seeds, the difference (treatment minus comparison) is taken on the same seed, subsample and splits (for H1, random forest minus logistic regression; for H2, isotonic minus no recalibration on the same fitted model). The 95% interval is a plain paired t(9) interval over those 10 differences on every dataset. Because seeds resample overlapping rows of the same pool, this interval measures variability over resplits of these samples, not population sampling variance, and the verdicts are scoped to these samples. Categories, in order of precedence: (1) 'no difference' if the whole interval lies within +/- the margin (Brier 0.001; ECE 0.005); (2) 'holds' if the whole interval lies on the predicted side; (3) 'contradicted' if it lies wholly on the other side; (4) otherwise 'no detectable difference (inconclusive)'. Overall: supported if it holds on at least 3 of the 4 datasets and is contradicted on none; contradicted if contradicted on at least 2; 'no difference' if 'no difference' on at least 3 and holds or is contradicted on none; otherwise inconclusive. All verdicts are scoped to these samples.
Platt scaling is applied to the logit of each model's predicted probability (one input scale for all models) and reported descriptively against none and isotonic; it is not a tested hypothesis.
contribution: Seed-resolved, per-model and per-dataset evidence on four named datasets, with the base model held fixed across recalibration methods with one confirmatory metric per hypothesis (ECE for H1, Brier score for H2a and H2b); a replication of a known calibration result (H1) and an extension of earlier evidence on isotonic recalibration for random forests and modern gradient boosting. It does not settle the disagreement among larger benchmarks.

tasks.title: Prior work on calibration of tabular classifiers and post-hoc recalibration (Platt; Zadrozny-Elkan; Niculescu-Mizil-Caruana; calibration metrics)

question.summary: Question passed review in round 3; minor findings answered afterwards or deferred to design.

design_stage_items: Preprocessing under 'library defaults': categorical encoding, scaling and max_iter for logistic regression (F6).
HistGradientBoosting's default early stopping switches on only above 10,000 training rows; state how this is handled so the procedure is the same on every dataset, or disclose the difference (F13).
Log-loss clipping epsilon, clip counts, and ECE tie handling at equal-mass bin edges (F14).
Whether each seed redraws the stratified subsample, and the resulting interval rule (F12).
Electricity (OpenML 151) is a time series; random splits put neighbouring time points on both sides. State this in design.threats and in the paper's limitations (F18).
